final_proof:
Proof. We first prove the result when both measures are finite. Put λ=μ+ν. Then λ is finite and ν≤λ. Work in the real Hilbert space L²(λ). For f∈L²(λ), define L(f)=∫_X f dν. This is well-defined on λ-almost-everywhere equivalence classes, since a λ-null set is also ν-null. Moreover, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

|L(f)|≤∫_X |f| dν≤ν(X)^{1/2}(∫_X |f|² dν)^{1/2}≤ν(X)^{1/2}‖f‖_{L²(λ)}.

Thus L is a bounded linear functional on L²(λ). By the Hilbert-space Riesz representation theorem, there is h∈L²(λ) such that

L(f)=∫_X fh dλ  for every f∈L²(λ).

(In the case ν(X)=0 this simply gives h=0.) Since λ is finite, 1_A∈L²(λ) for every A∈Σ. Taking f=1_A therefore yields

ν(A)=∫_A h dλ.   (1)

We next show that 0≤h≤1 λ-almost everywhere. If B={h<0} had positive λ-measure, then (1) would give ν(B)=∫_B h dλ<0. To justify the strict inequality explicitly, B is the union of the sets {h≤−1/n}; one of these would have positive measure. This contradicts ν(B)≥0. Similarly, if C={h>1} had positive λ-measure, then C is the union of the sets {h≥1+1/n}, so for some n,

ν(C)=∫_C h dλ>λ(C),

contrary to ν≤λ. Changing h on a λ-null set, we may and do suppose that 0≤h≤1 everywhere.

Because μ=λ−ν, equation (1) gives, for every A∈Σ,

μ(A)=∫_A (1−h) dλ.   (2)

Consequently, first for nonnegative simple functions and then, by monotone convergence, for every nonnegative measurable φ,

∫_X φ dμ=∫_X φ(1−h) dλ.   (3)

Let N={h=1}. Equation (2) gives μ(N)=0. Since ν≪μ, also ν(N)=0, and hence λ(N)=μ(N)+ν(N)=0. Define

g(x)={h(x)/(1−h(x)) if x∉N, and 0 if x∈N}.

This is a measurable function from X to [0,∞). Applying (3) to φ=1_A g and using λ(N)=0 gives, for every A∈Σ,

∫_A g dμ=∫_A g(1−h) dλ=∫_{A\N} h dλ=∫_A h dλ=ν(A).

This proves the assertion in the finite-measure case.

Now suppose μ and ν are σ-finite. Choose measurable sets E_1,E_2,… and F_1,F_2,… covering X such that μ(E_i)<∞ and ν(F_j)<∞. The countable family {E_i∩F_j:i,j≥1} covers X, and each of its members has finite measure for both μ and ν. Enumerate this family as D_1,D_2,… and disjointify it by setting C_1=D_1 and C_n=D_n\(D_1∪⋯∪D_{n−1}) for n≥2. Then the C_n are measurable, pairwise disjoint, cover X, and satisfy μ(C_n)<∞ and ν(C_n)<∞.

For each n, apply the finite case on the measurable space (C_n,{A∩C_n:A∈Σ}) to the restrictions of μ and ν. Absolute continuity is inherited by these restrictions, so there is a measurable g_n:C_n→[0,∞) such that

ν(A∩C_n)=∫_{A∩C_n} g_n dμ  for every A∈Σ.

Define g on X by g=g_n on C_n. The countable measurable partition makes g measurable. For every A∈Σ, countable additivity of ν and additivity of the nonnegative integral over a measurable partition give

ν(A)=Σ_{n=1}^∞ν(A∩C_n)=Σ_{n=1}^∞∫_{A∩C_n}g dμ=∫_A g dμ.

It remains to prove uniqueness. Suppose g_1,g_2:X→[0,∞) are measurable and each represents ν. By σ-finiteness of ν, choose measurable Y_1,Y_2,… covering X with ν(Y_n)<∞. Fix n and put B_n={g_1>g_2}∩Y_n. The representing identities imply

∫_{B_n}g_1 dμ=ν(B_n)=∫_{B_n}g_2 dμ<∞.

Both integrals being finite, subtraction is legitimate, and therefore ∫_{B_n}(g_1−g_2)dμ=0. The integrand is strictly positive on B_n, so μ(B_n)=0: indeed, B_n is the union over k≥1 of B_n∩{g_1−g_2≥1/k}, and each of the latter sets must have μ-measure zero. Since the Y_n cover X, {g_1>g_2}=⋃_n B_n is μ-null. Interchanging g_1 and g_2 shows that {g_2>g_1} is also μ-null. Hence g_1=g_2 μ-almost everywhere. ∎
